newsitem.title: INDIA: India political drama seen as failure of democracy.
newsitem.headline: India political drama seen as failure of democracy.

text.p: A dramatic political saga involving a disgraced politician who installed his unschooled wife as his successor has made a mockery of democracy in one of India's biggest states, political analysts said on Wednesday.
Laloo Prasad Yadav resigned as chief minister of the poor eastern state of Bihar and anointed Rabri Devi, a housewife and mother of nine, as his successor last Friday.
"The entire situation is a farce," said analyst Ashis Nandy of the Centre for Study of Developing Societies.

"In the long term, the implication is that this is the kind of people we will have to deal with, who are coming from the peripheries of society, tasting power for the first time and willing to cling very desperately to it at all costs," he said.

A court in the state capital Patna on Wednesday ordered the detention of Yadav, a charismatic low-caste leader who once headed Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral's party and had embarrassed the government by refusing to resign.
India's federal police have indicted Yadav in a $280 million embezzlement scandal. He says he is innocent.
His inexperienced wife's sudden rise to the head of the mineral-rich but economically backward state stunned commentators and sparked sharp criticism.

"The objection to Ms Devi's anointment is not so much because she could not address the (state) assembly in style or because she does not possess high educational qualifications," the conservative Hindu newspaper said in an uncharacteristically strong editorial.

"It is objectionable because a novice in politics was thrust upon the people of Bihar by Mr Laloo Yadav only to ensure his own rule by proxy, to enable him to continue with all that he had done hitherto in scuttling the investigations in the fodder scam," the daily said.
On Tuesday Devi expanded her cabinet to a breathtaking 75 ministers in an apparent bid to keep many of her husband's deputies happy.
Newspapers seized swiftly upon what was perhaps the largest cabinet ever in an Indian state.

"Bihar governor A.R. Kidwai had the look of a marathon runner just past the finish line after he administered the oath of office and secrecy to 61 new ministers," the Indian Express said in a front page article headlined "Rabri Devi installs mother of all ministries in Bihar".
The Hindu said: "As if it were not enough to render governance into a farcical exercise, the cabinet expansion undertaken by Ms Rabri Devi...is simply outrageous."
The drama in Bihar stirred bitter debate in India's parliament, with even Home (Interior) Minister Indrajit Gupta saying: "It is a glaring example of the abyss into which the country is sinking."

Under fire from the main opposition Bharatiya Janata Party for not sacking Yadav and imposing direct federal rule over Bihar, Gupta admitted that Yadav's decision to install his wife had taken everybody by surprise and said he found it "utterly distressing".

Former police chief Ved Marwah said Yadav had exhausted every possible means of evading arrest since he was indicted in April, by filing for preventive bail and appealing to even the Supreme Court to consider it.

"Now he will be in jail for a week while the police question him," Marwah said, referring to a police guest house that the state government has converted into a temporary prison for Yadav until August 6.
"He is a very, very clever politician, and he obviously wants to retain his hold over power, to be the one distributing the loaves and fish," Marwah said.
